title: The Best Test Prep Schools Ignore
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Kevin Stinehart argues that schools are chasing the wrong kind of test preparation. The executive function and self-regulation skills that unstructured play develops are precisely the cognitive capacities that standardised tests actually measure, yet schools systematically cut recess and free play in favour of direct test-prep activities that address only surface-level content. Citing research on self-discipline as a stronger predictor of academic success than IQ, Stinehart introduces the 'Play Deprivation Delay Theory' and references a Long Island University study in which students who attended a Play Club scored measurably higher on reading and mathematics assessments than peers who did not. The article challenges the assumption that rigorous academic preparation and play are in tension, arguing instead that play is preparation — and that the most evidence-based test-prep strategy a school can adopt is protecting children's time to play.
points: Self-discipline is a stronger predictor of academic achievement than IQ — meaning the self-regulation skills built through play have direct, measurable effects on test performance.

The 'Play Deprivation Delay Theory' holds that cutting unstructured play does not simply remove a recreational benefit; it actively delays development of the executive function capacities tests are designed to measure.
A Long Island University study found that students who participated in a Play Club scored higher on both reading and mathematics assessments than peers without that play intervention.
Schools that replace recess with test-prep drills are not being rigorous — they are trading a high-yield developmental investment for a low-yield content rehearsal.

Play builds working memory, inhibitory control, and cognitive flexibility — the same competencies that allow students to manage test anxiety, sustain attention, and apply knowledge flexibly under pressure.
quotes: Self-discipline predicts academic success more reliably than IQ. The child who can regulate her attention and delay gratification will outperform the child who simply knows more.
We have confused test preparation with test performance. Drilling content addresses the surface. Play builds the cognitive architecture that lets students use that content under pressure.
The Play Deprivation Delay Theory is not a soft claim about childhood happiness. It is a developmental argument: remove play, delay the executive function development that tests actually measure.
Schools that cut recess to make room for more instruction are not being serious about achievement. They are being serious about the wrong thing.
